clue.text: Evening suit for places of entertainment (two words)

parts.note: night is the evening time, so evening stands for night
clubs is one of the four suits in a pack of playing cards

explanation.surface: Someone puts on an evening suit before heading out to be entertained.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Evening suit' reads as formal wear, but it splits into two pieces: the time of day and a suit of cards.
explanation.definitionFit: Late-opening venues with music, dancing and drink are classic places of entertainment.

clue.text: This and this are side by side

definitions.text: This and this are side by side

parts.words: This and this are side by side
parts.note: the phrase 'this and this' becomes the idiom for two contestants dead level, the word said twice with 'and' between

explanation.surface: A riddle about two things lying side by side.
explanation.walkthrough: The idiom 'neck and neck' means level in a race; the clue swaps the word for 'this'.
explanation.definitionFit: In a horse race, runners level with each other are said to be this word 'and' this word again.

clue.text: Where Tennyson was alone

parts.note: points to the line in Tennyson's poem Maud where the speaker waits by himself for his love

explanation.surface: A literary question about the poet Tennyson's solitude.
explanation.walkthrough: Tennyson's Maud: 'Come into the garden, Maud ... I am here at the gate alone.'
explanation.definitionFit: The speaker of Maud says he stands alone at the garden entrance, which is the place asked for.

clue.text: Expression of mirth .

parts.note: a plain description of a sound people make when they snigger or giggle

explanation.surface: A bare description of a giggle.
explanation.definitionFit: It is an old spelling of the sound of a snigger, a little laugh of amusement.

clue.text: Kentish castle in Yorkshire

definitions.meaning: a famous moated castle near Maidstone in the county of Kent shares its name with a northern city
a large city in the county of Yorkshire in northern England

explanation.surface: A castle in Kent that is somehow placed in Yorkshire, which seems contradictory.
explanation.walkthrough: Kent is a county in south-east England and Yorkshire a county in the north; the castle and the city share one name.
explanation.definitionFit: Leeds Castle stands in Kent, and the city of the same name lies in Yorkshire.

clue.text: Not parallel lines of understanding (two words)

parts.note: 'understanding' is read as the limbs one stands on, and 'not parallel' describes them curving outward

explanation.surface: An abstract phrase about lines of understanding that diverge.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Understanding' sounds like comprehension, but it means what you stand on, your limbs; bowed ones are not parallel.
explanation.definitionFit: Bowed lower limbs curve apart rather than running straight and parallel.

clue.text: Glad

parts.note: a single-word definition: an old poetic word meaning pleased or willing

explanation.definitionFit: It is an archaic word for pleased or willing, as in 'I would fain go'.

clue.text: A long tale turn into assertion

indicators.note: turn into tells us to change these letters into a new word

parts.note: the printed words are taken as written for the anagram, with the extra I the setter meant to include

explanation.surface: Someone spins a long story into a claim.
explanation.walkthrough: 'turn into' signals an anagram, but A LONG TALE has only nine letters; the answer needs an I as well, which the clue as printed does not supply.
explanation.definitionFit: An allegation is a claim made without proof, a kind of assertion.

clue.text: What to put on a night mare

definitions.text: What to put on a night mare

parts.words: What to put on a night mare
parts.note: 'night mare' is split so a bad dream becomes a female horse out after dark that needs dressing for bed

explanation.surface: Advice about calming a nightmare.
explanation.walkthrough: 'nightmare' is broken into 'night mare', a horse at night; you dress her in bed-wear.
explanation.definitionFit: A garment worn in bed is what you would put on anything ready for the night.

clue.text: Get hold of a copper

parts.note: describes an article made cheaply to grab a small coin from the buyer, read as seizing a policeman

explanation.surface: Someone trying to find a police officer.
explanation.walkthrough: 'copper' looks like a policeman but is a copper coin; catch = get hold of, penny = copper, and the whole means cheap goods made to grab money.
explanation.definitionFit: Trashy goods designed only to tempt buyers into spending a coin are described this way.

clue.text: Collectors should not on these days

definitions.text: Collectors should not on these days

parts.words: Collectors should not on these days
parts.note: charity street collections are held on named days, and 'should not' wants a verb meaning tire or droop

explanation.surface: A rule for charity collectors on certain days.
explanation.walkthrough: On charity collection days in Britain, collectors gave out little paper tokens; the same word means to grow weary, which collectors should not do.
explanation.definitionFit: The word both names those charity days and means to tire, which collectors must not do.

clue.text: He's on the mend but not very satisfactorily

definitions.text: He's on the mend but not very satisfactorily

parts.words: He's on the mend but not very satisfactorily
parts.note: 'on the mend' suggests recovery but means a man who mends pots and pans, and fiddles at repairs clumsily

explanation.surface: A patient recovering only slowly.
explanation.walkthrough: 'on the mend' suggests a patient getting better, but he is an itinerant mender of pots, and the verb means to fiddle with repairs ineffectively.
explanation.definitionFit: A travelling mender of pots, whose name is also the verb for unskilled fiddling repair.

clue.text: Nocturnally delightful but matutinally ominous to the shepherd (two words)

definitions.text: Nocturnally delightful but matutinally ominous to the shepherd

parts.words: Nocturnally delightful but matutinally ominous to the shepherd
parts.note: recalls the weather proverb in which the evening colour of the heavens is a shepherd's delight and the morning colour his warning

explanation.surface: A shepherd's mood at night and in the morning.
explanation.walkthrough: The proverb: 'Red sky at night, shepherd's delight; red sky in the morning, shepherd's warning.' Matutinally means in the morning.
explanation.definitionFit: A crimson sunset or dawn is what the shepherd's weather proverb describes.

clue.text: Found in certain Gothic remains

indicators.note: in tells us the answer sits inside the run of letters of certain Gothic

explanation.surface: Something discovered among old Gothic ruins.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Found' looks like a past tense of find but is the verb to cast metal; a cast bar is what founding makes. 'remains' links the parts.
explanation.definitionFit: To found metal is to cast it, and a cast bar of gold is the product.

clue.text: Aladdin's perhaps: (two words)

parts.note: Aladdin's famous possession housed a genie, so it can be described as a light holding a supernatural being

explanation.surface: A reference to Aladdin's magic possession.
explanation.walkthrough: In the tale, Aladdin's lamp held a genie, a spirit; the name also means a lamp burning methylated spirit.
explanation.definitionFit: A lamp fuelled by alcohol shares a name with Aladdin's genie-holding lamp.

clue.text: Misers do what sailors may get

definitions.meaning: misers value cash above all, so they hold it dear
naval crews were once paid a share of a captured enemy ship's value

explanation.surface: Misers and sailors both care about money.
explanation.walkthrough: Read as a verb, misers 'prize money'; read as a noun, it is the share of a captured ship paid to the crew.
explanation.definitionFit: Misers treasure cash, and seamen once earned bounty from captured vessels.

clue.text: This creature has more than one spine

definitions.text: This creature has more than one spine

parts.words: This creature has more than one spine
parts.note: 'spine' suggests a backbone, but here it means a quill, and this animal is covered in them

explanation.surface: A biological oddity: an animal with several backbones.
explanation.walkthrough: 'spine' suggests a backbone, of which every animal has one; here it means the sharp quills this rodent is covered in.
explanation.definitionFit: This rodent is covered in sharp quills, many spines rather than one backbone.

clue.text: Conrad wrote tales of it

parts.note: Joseph Conrad's short-story collection Tales of ... names the missing word

explanation.surface: A literary note about Joseph Conrad's stories.
explanation.walkthrough: Joseph Conrad published Tales of Unrest in 1898.
explanation.definitionFit: The title of Conrad's 1898 story collection completes 'Tales of' with a word for agitation.

clue.text: Choleric

parts.note: a single-word definition meaning quick to anger, from the old humour of yellow bile

explanation.definitionFit: Choleric people are bad-tempered and easily annoyed.

clue.text: With this sailing boat Jack provided many capital finishes

definitions.meaning: Jack ... was a notorious English hangman, so he ended many lives in capital punishment

explanation.surface: A sailor named Jack finishing many races in style aboard his boat.
explanation.walkthrough: 'capital finishes' sounds like excellent endings, but means executions; Jack Ketch was the hangman of 17th-century England.
explanation.definitionFit: It is a two-masted vessel, and the surname of a famous English executioner.

clue.text: Safety first with this very often

definitions.text: Safety first with this very often

parts.words: Safety first with this very often
parts.note: 'Safety first' reads as a slogan but means the word safety placed before this one, as in a guarded shaving blade

explanation.surface: A safety slogan about a dangerous tool.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Safety first' reads as a motto, but means 'safety' comes in front: the safety razor.
explanation.definitionFit: A shaving blade is very often a safety one, with a guard.

clue.text: Where liquid assets are kept on deposit

definitions.text: Where liquid assets are kept on deposit

parts.words: Where liquid assets are kept on deposit
parts.note: 'liquid assets' sounds like money in the bank, but means water, held in store

explanation.surface: A bank where cash savings are held.
explanation.walkthrough: 'liquid assets' and 'deposit' sound like banking, but the assets are literally water stored in a lake.
explanation.definitionFit: A large man-made lake stores water until it is drawn off for use.

clue.text: Hardly the prison in which a prisoner might serve a life sentence

definitions.text: Hardly the prison in which a prisoner might serve a life sentence

parts.words: Hardly the prison in which a prisoner might serve a life sentence
parts.note: the name of a New York jail, also burial chambers where one stays only after life has ended

explanation.surface: A remark about which jail would hold a lifer.
explanation.walkthrough: The Tombs is a New York prison; but tombs hold people after life is over, so no one serves a life sentence in them.
explanation.definitionFit: Burial vaults hold the dead, and the same name belongs to a famous Manhattan jail.

clue.text: Fishes that—-in the deep Know no such liberty " (Lovelace)

definitions.text: Fishes that—-in the deep Know no such liberty " (Lovelace)

parts.words: Fishes that—-in the deep Know no such liberty " (Lovelace)
parts.note: a fill-in-the-blank from Richard Lovelace's poem To Althea, from Prison, where the missing verb means to drink

explanation.surface: A line of poetry with a word missing.
explanation.walkthrough: Lovelace's To Althea, from Prison: 'Fishes that tipple in the deep / Know no such liberty.'
explanation.definitionFit: The missing verb means to drink habitually, as fish swim in water.

clue.text: Simple Marryat character, blue on departure

definitions.meaning: Captain Frederick Marryat wrote the novel named after its hero, whose surname is Simple
the Blue ... is the flag a ship hoists when about to sail

explanation.surface: A naive character in Marryat feeling sad as he leaves.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Simple' and 'blue' look like adjectives (naive, sad) but are parts of names: Marryat's novel Peter Simple, and the Blue Peter flag flown before sailing.
explanation.definitionFit: It is the first name of Marryat's hero Simple, and completes the Blue flag flown by departing ships.

clue.text: A girl in danger conceals her

indicators.note: conceals tells us the answer is tucked away inside the letters of the words before it

explanation.surface: A girl in peril keeps herself out of sight.
explanation.walkthrough: 'her' refers to a girl whose name lies inside 'girl in danger'.
explanation.definitionFit: The pronoun stands for a woman, here one with a girl's first name.

clue.text: Associated in literature with Geraint

parts.note: Geraint is the Arthurian knight whose wife is paired with him in Tennyson's Idylls of the King

explanation.surface: A literary note about the knight Geraint.
explanation.walkthrough: Tennyson's Idylls of the King include 'Geraint and Enid'.
explanation.definitionFit: Geraint's faithful wife shares the title of Tennyson's idyll with him.

clue.text: Material for Scotswoman or Frenchman

definitions.meaning: a common female name in Scotland and a common male name in France

explanation.surface: A fabric suited to a Scottish woman or a French man.
explanation.walkthrough: The same four letters are a cotton cloth, a Scottish girl's name, and the French form of John.
explanation.definitionFit: It is a twilled cotton fabric and a first name, female in Scotland, male in France.

clue.text: Mr. F.'s perhaps

parts.note: Mr F.'s relative is the eccentric old lady in Dickens's Little Dorrit, known only by that relation

explanation.surface: A guess about something belonging to a Mr F.
explanation.walkthrough: In Dickens's Little Dorrit, a dotty old woman is known only as 'Mr F.'s Aunt'.
explanation.definitionFit: Dickens names the character only as Mr F.'s female relative, his father's sister.

clue.text: In best cane (anag.)

indicators.note: the abbreviation anag. tells the solver to rearrange the words in brackets

explanation.surface: A bare instruction to rearrange three words.
explanation.walkthrough: The clue gives no definition, only the instruction to rearrange IN BEST CANE; the result means self-denial.
explanation.definitionFit: The letters rearranged give a word meaning refraining from drink or indulgence.

clue.text: Settles in a foreign country

definitions.meaning: settles a bill means hands over money for it

explanation.surface: Someone goes to live abroad.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Settles in' looks like making a home, but 'in' is a link; 'a foreign country' is the French word for country.
explanation.definitionFit: To settle a bill is to pay it, and the French word for country is spelt the same.

clue.text: noisy spot with grizzly associations possibly (two words)

definitions.text: noisy spot with grizzly associations possibly

parts.words: noisy spot with grizzly associations possibly
parts.note: 'grizzly' points to a large animal, and the place is an old site for baiting it, now any rowdy scene

explanation.surface: A loud place perhaps connected with bears.
explanation.walkthrough: Bears were once baited in enclosures for sport; the name came to mean any scene of uproar.
explanation.definitionFit: Once a place where animals were baited, the name now means any rowdy, disorderly scene.
